title: Irregularly irregular palpitations
presentingComplaint: Sudden onset of a fluttering, irregular heartbeat this morning, with mild breathlessness on walking.
history: Palpitations began abruptly at about 07:00 and have been continuous since
Hypertension for twelve years, on amlodipine
Two units of alcohol most evenings; three glasses of wine last night
No previous documented arrhythmia; no chest pain, no syncope
symptoms: Breathless on climbing one flight of stairs
examinationFindings: Pulse irregularly irregular with varying volume; apex rate exceeds the radial rate
Jugular venous pressure not raised, with no visible a waves
Heart sounds of varying intensity; no murmur

vitals.bedside: Comfortable but aware of every beat. The monitor's rate readout jumps around because the ventricular response is genuinely irregular.

ecg.rate: Ventricular rate averaging 118 bpm, but varying beat to beat — count over six seconds
ecg.rhythm: Irregularly irregular, with no repeating pattern to the R–R intervals
ecg.pWaves: Absent. The baseline shows fine fibrillatory undulation, best seen in V1
ecg.prInterval: Not measurable — there are no P waves to measure from
ecg.qrs: 0.09 s, narrow and of normal morphology
ecg.stSegment: Isoelectric, with minor rate-related upsloping depression
ecg.tWaves: Upright, varying slightly in amplitude with the changing cycle length
keyFindings: No organised atrial activity: no P waves, only a fibrillatory baseline
Irregularly irregular ventricular response — no repeating pattern at all
Narrow QRS complexes, confirming conduction through the normal His–Purkinje system
Beat-to-beat variation in the pulse waveform, because short cycles allow less ventricular filling

interpretation: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response at an average of 118 bpm, with a narrow QRS and no acute ischaemic change.

auscultation.note: S1 varies in intensity from beat to beat because the position of the mitral leaflets at the onset of systole depends on the length of the preceding diastole.
No fourth heart sound — there cannot be one, because S4 is produced by atrial contraction and the atria are fibrillating.
No murmur. Listen for aortic stenosis in any older patient with new atrial fibrillation, since valve disease is a common substrate.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation
options.feedback: Correct. Absent P waves, a fibrillatory baseline and an irregularly irregular ventricular response are the three defining features.

options.text: Atrial flutter with variable block
options.feedback: Flutter with variable block is also irregular, but the baseline shows organised sawtooth waves at about 300 per minute rather than chaotic undulation.

options.text: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
options.feedback: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular but has visible P waves of at least three different morphologies. There are no P waves here.

options.text: Sinus rhythm with frequent ectopic beats
options.feedback: Frequent ectopics interrupt an otherwise regular underlying rhythm with identifiable P waves. Neither is present.

questions.explanation: Three questions settle it: are there P waves, is the baseline organised, and is the ventricular response irregularly irregular?

questions.prompt: How should the ventricular rate be measured in this rhythm?

options.text: Count the QRS complexes in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10
options.feedback: Correct. Dividing 300 by large squares assumes a regular rhythm, which this is not.

options.text: Divide 300 by the number of large squares between two adjacent R waves
options.feedback: That gives the instantaneous rate for one cycle only, and every cycle here is a different length.

options.text: Use the atrial rate, since it is more consistent
options.feedback: The atrial rate in fibrillation is 400–600 per minute and is not what determines cardiac output.

options.text: Take the radial pulse rate
options.feedback: The radial rate underestimates the true ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation, because short cycles produce beats too weak to reach the wrist — the pulse deficit.

questions.explanation: Whenever a rhythm is irregular, average over at least six seconds. And auscultate at the apex rather than palpating the radial pulse.

questions.prompt: The QRS complexes are narrow at 0.09 s. What does that tell you?

options.text: The ventricles are being activated through the normal conducting system
options.feedback: Correct. A narrow QRS means the impulse reached the ventricles through the His–Purkinje system, so the rhythm originates at or above the atrioventricular node.

options.text: The rhythm must be ventricular in origin
options.feedback: The opposite: ventricular rhythms have broad QRS complexes because activation spreads slowly, cell to cell.

options.text: There is a bundle branch block
options.feedback: Bundle branch block widens the QRS to 0.12 s or more.

options.text: It excludes any structural heart disease
options.feedback: QRS width says nothing about structure — plenty of structurally abnormal hearts have narrow complexes.

questions.explanation: QRS width is the single most useful discriminator between supraventricular and ventricular origin, and it should be checked on every tracing.

questions.prompt: Given the history, the observations and the tracing, what is the most likely interpretation?

options.text: New-onset atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, possibly alcohol-related
options.feedback: Correct. Abrupt onset, a clear temporal relationship with alcohol, hypertension as a substrate, and a classic tracing.

options.text: Ventricular tachycardia
options.feedback: Ventricular tachycardia is broad-complex and usually regular. These complexes are narrow and the rhythm is irregular.

options.text: Acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction
options.feedback: There is no ST elevation and no chest pain. Atrial fibrillation can complicate infarction, but nothing here points to it.

options.text: Complete heart block with an escape rhythm
options.feedback: Complete heart block gives a slow, regular ventricular escape rhythm with dissociated P waves.

questions.explanation: The tracing gives you the rhythm; the history gives you the trigger and the substrate. Both are needed before the encounter is complete.

questions.prompt: Beyond rate control, which assessment is essential in this educational scenario?

options.text: Formal thromboembolic risk assessment to decide about anticoagulation
options.feedback: Correct. Stroke prevention is the intervention that changes outcome most in atrial fibrillation, and risk is assessed with a validated score rather than by impression.

options.text: Immediate DC cardioversion regardless of symptom duration
options.feedback: Cardioversion is reserved for haemodynamic instability, or is planned with attention to the duration of the episode and anticoagulation status because of thromboembolic risk.

options.text: Start an antiplatelet agent instead of anticoagulation
options.feedback: Antiplatelet therapy is substantially less effective than anticoagulation for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation and is not a substitute for it.

options.text: No further assessment is needed once the rate is below 100 bpm
options.feedback: Rate control treats symptoms. It does not address the risk of stroke.

questions.explanation: Educational scenario only. Anticoagulation and rhythm decisions follow validated risk scores and current guidelines, applied by the treating team.

explanation: Atrial fibrillation. The atria are depolarising chaotically at 400–600 per minute from multiple re-entrant wavelets, so there is no coordinated atrial contraction and no P wave — only a fibrillatory baseline, seen best in V1. The atrioventricular node is bombarded and conducts unpredictably, which is what makes the ventricular response irregularly irregular. The QRS stays narrow because conduction below the node is normal. The loss of atrial systole removes roughly a fifth of ventricular filling and, more importantly, allows stasis in the left atrial appendage — which is why the central clinical question is thromboembolic risk rather than rate.
learningObjectives: Recognise atrial fibrillation from absent P waves plus an irregularly irregular ventricular response
Use lead V1 to examine atrial activity
Measure rate over six seconds whenever the rhythm is irregular
Explain why stroke prevention, not rate, is the decision that changes outcome
clinicalContext: The ECG establishes the rhythm. It cannot establish how long the patient has been in it, whether there is structural heart disease, or what the stroke risk is — that requires the history, echocardiography and a validated risk score.

title: A regular tachycardia at exactly 150
presentingComplaint: Three days of breathlessness on exertion and a persistent fast heartbeat.
history: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, ex-smoker of 40 pack-years
Admitted twice in the past year with infective exacerbations
No chest pain; ankle swelling for a week
symptoms: Continuous awareness of a fast, regular heartbeat
examinationFindings: Mildly tachypnoeic, speaking in short sentences
Jugular venous pressure raised with rapid flutter waves visible
Bilateral pitting ankle oedema; scattered wheeze

vitals.bedside: Breathless but not distressed. A ventricular rate sitting stubbornly at almost exactly 150 should always make you look for flutter waves.

ecg.rate: Ventricular rate 150 bpm; atrial rate approximately 300 per minute
ecg.pWaves: No discrete P waves. A continuous sawtooth flutter baseline with no isoelectric interval, negative in the inferior leads
ecg.prInterval: Not applicable — flutter waves, not P waves
ecg.stSegment: Difficult to assess, because flutter waves deform the segment. Do not over-call ischaemia here
ecg.tWaves: Superimposed on flutter waves; individually hard to define
keyFindings: A ventricular rate of almost exactly 150 bpm — always suspect flutter with 2:1 block
Sawtooth atrial activity at about 300 per minute, best seen in II, III and aVF
Alternate flutter waves are hidden inside the QRS and the T wave, which is why they are so easily missed
The QRS is narrow: this is a supraventricular rhythm

interpretation: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular conduction, atrial rate approximately 300 per minute and ventricular rate 150 bpm, with a narrow QRS.

auscultation.note: Regular, fast heart sounds of constant intensity — unlike atrial fibrillation, where S1 varies from beat to beat.
Nothing added. Look at the neck rather than listening: rapid flutter waves are often visible in the jugular venous pulse.

options.text: Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction
options.feedback: Correct. Organised sawtooth atrial activity at about 300 per minute with every second impulse conducted gives a ventricular rate of 150.

options.text: Sinus tachycardia
options.feedback: Sinus tachycardia has discrete upright P waves in lead II with an isoelectric baseline between them, and the rate varies with activity rather than sitting fixed at 150.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation
options.feedback: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with a chaotic baseline. This rhythm is strikingly regular and the atrial activity is organised.

options.text: Ventricular tachycardia
options.feedback: Ventricular tachycardia is broad-complex. The QRS here is 0.09 s.

questions.explanation: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 bpm is atrial flutter until you have proved otherwise by finding the flutter waves.

questions.prompt: How do you demonstrate the flutter waves hidden inside the QRS complexes?

options.text: Increase atrioventricular block transiently — vagal manoeuvres or adenosine — and watch the baseline
options.feedback: Correct. Slowing conduction through the node exposes the atrial activity without terminating the flutter, because the circuit is in the atrium.

options.text: Give a synchronised DC shock and look at the tracing afterwards
options.feedback: Cardioversion is a treatment, not a diagnostic manoeuvre, and it is not used simply to clarify a rhythm in a stable patient.

options.text: Increase the paper speed to 50 mm/s
options.feedback: This does spread the complexes out and can help, but it does not reveal waves buried inside the QRS.

options.text: Record only lead V6
options.feedback: V6 has the smallest atrial signal of any lead. The inferior leads and V1 are where flutter waves are seen.

questions.explanation: Adenosine in a regular narrow tachycardia is both diagnostic and potentially therapeutic: it terminates nodal re-entry and unmasks flutter.

questions.prompt: Why is the QRS narrow despite a ventricular rate of 150?

options.text: Because the impulse still reaches the ventricles through the His–Purkinje system
options.feedback: Correct. The flutter circuit is confined to the atrium; below the atrioventricular node conduction is entirely normal.

options.text: Because the rate is too fast for the QRS to widen
options.feedback: Rate does not narrow a QRS. If anything, very fast rates can produce rate-related aberrant conduction and widen it.

options.text: Because the atria are contributing to ventricular depolarisation
options.feedback: The atria never depolarise the ventricles directly; the impulse must pass through the conduction system.

options.text: Because there is 2:1 block
options.feedback: The conduction ratio determines the ventricular rate, not the QRS width.

questions.explanation: Narrow QRS means normal ventricular activation, which localises the arrhythmia to the atria or the atrioventricular junction.

questions.prompt: Putting the chronic lung disease, the raised venous pressure and the tracing together, what is the most likely interpretation?

options.text: Atrial flutter in the context of chronic lung disease and right atrial stretch
options.feedback: Correct. Chronic lung disease raises right heart pressures and dilates the right atrium, which is the substrate for the typical cavotricuspid isthmus-dependent flutter circuit.

options.text: Sinus tachycardia secondary to hypoxia
options.feedback: Hypoxia is present, but the atrial activity is organised at 300 per minute with a sawtooth baseline — this is not sinus.

options.text: Acute coronary syndrome
options.feedback: There is no chest pain and no ischaemic ST change that can be interpreted through the flutter waves.

options.text: Pulmonary embolism causing right heart strain
options.feedback: Worth considering in any breathless patient with a new atrial arrhythmia, but the three-day history in known chronic lung disease with fluid overload fits flutter secondary to atrial stretch better.

questions.explanation: Atrial arrhythmias arise where atria are stretched. The lungs, the valves and the ventricles are all worth examining when flutter appears.

questions.prompt: Which statement about management in this educational scenario is most accurate?

options.text: Thromboembolic risk in atrial flutter is managed as it is in atrial fibrillation
options.feedback: Correct. Flutter carries a comparable stroke risk, and the same anticoagulation assessment applies — a point that is frequently forgotten.

options.text: Atrial flutter does not require any consideration of anticoagulation
options.feedback: This is a common and dangerous misconception. Flutter and fibrillation are assessed the same way, and the two often coexist.

options.text: Adenosine reliably terminates atrial flutter
options.feedback: Adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node. The flutter circuit is in the atrium, so it unmasks the flutter rather than stopping it.

options.text: Rate control in flutter is usually easier to achieve than in fibrillation
options.feedback: The opposite is generally true: flutter is often more resistant to rate control, which is one reason ablation of the isthmus is attractive.

questions.explanation: Educational scenario only. Anticoagulation, rate control and ablation decisions follow current guidelines and specialist assessment.

explanation: Typical atrial flutter is a single macro-re-entrant circuit rotating around the tricuspid annulus at about 300 per minute. Because the circuit is continuous there is no isoelectric baseline: the atrial deflections run into one another as a sawtooth, negative in II, III and aVF and positive in V1. The atrioventricular node cannot conduct 300 impulses a minute, so it blocks — most often two to one, giving the characteristic ventricular rate of 150. That fixed rate is the clue, because alternate flutter waves hide inside the QRS and the T wave and are genuinely easy to miss. Transient atrioventricular block, from a vagal manoeuvre or adenosine, exposes them.
learningObjectives: Treat a regular narrow tachycardia at 150 bpm as flutter until proved otherwise
Identify sawtooth flutter waves in the inferior leads and V1
Explain why increasing atrioventricular block unmasks rather than terminates flutter
Apply the same thromboembolic risk assessment to flutter as to fibrillation
clinicalContext: The ECG shows the rhythm and the conduction ratio. It does not show the atrial size, the right heart pressures or the stroke risk, all of which need separate assessment.

title: Abrupt onset, very fast, very regular
presentingComplaint: Sudden onset of a racing heartbeat 40 minutes ago while sitting at her desk, with a fluttering sensation in the neck.
history: Three similar episodes over two years, each starting and stopping abruptly and lasting minutes
Previous episodes stopped spontaneously or with breath-holding
No structural heart disease; no medication
symptoms: Racing, regular palpitations of instantaneous onset
Mild light-headedness but no loss of consciousness
examinationFindings: Anxious, alert, warm and well perfused
Regular pulse, too fast to count accurately at the wrist
Prominent regular neck pulsation — the 'frog sign' of simultaneous atrial and ventricular contraction
Heart sounds fast and regular; no murmur

vitals.bedside: Alert and talking, with a stable blood pressure. Stable enough for vagal manoeuvres first — a sudden onset and offset is the history that defines this rhythm.

ecg.rhythm: Absolutely regular — the R–R intervals do not vary at all
ecg.pWaves: No P wave visible before the QRS. A small deflection distorts the terminal QRS — a retrograde P wave conducted backwards to the atria
ecg.stSegment: Up to 1 mm of downsloping depression in the inferolateral leads — common at this rate and usually not ischaemic
ecg.tWaves: Small and partly merged with the following P wave
keyFindings: A very fast, absolutely regular, narrow-complex tachycardia
No discernible preceding P wave; retrograde atrial activation distorts the end of the QRS
Rate-related ST depression, which frequently resolves completely once the rhythm terminates
Abrupt onset and abrupt offset in the history — the hallmark of re-entry

interpretation: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 186 bpm with no visible preceding P wave — findings consistent with atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia. Rate-related ST depression is present and should be reassessed after the rhythm converts.

auscultation.note: Very fast, regular and of constant intensity. Diastole is so short that S2 and the next S1 nearly merge.
No added sound. The regular cannon waves in the neck come from the atria contracting against closed atrioventricular valves.

options.text: Supraventricular tachycardia — most likely atrioventricular nodal re-entry
options.feedback: Correct. A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 186 bpm with abrupt onset and no preceding P wave is nodal re-entry until proved otherwise.

options.text: Sinus tachycardia
options.feedback: Sinus tachycardia rarely exceeds about 220 minus age at rest, has visible upright P waves, and warms up and cools down rather than starting instantly.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
options.feedback: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular. This rhythm is absolutely regular.

options.text: Ventricular tachycardia
options.feedback: The QRS is 0.085 s. Ventricular tachycardia is broad-complex, above 0.12 s.

questions.explanation: Regular, narrow, very fast, no P waves, instantaneous onset — that combination is re-entry involving the atrioventricular node.

questions.prompt: Where are the atrial complexes in this rhythm?

options.text: Buried within or just after the QRS, because atria and ventricles are activated almost simultaneously
options.feedback: Correct. In typical nodal re-entry the retrograde P wave is hidden in the QRS or appears as a pseudo-R′ in V1 or a pseudo-S in the inferior leads.

options.text: Immediately before each QRS with a short PR interval
options.feedback: That would suggest an atrial tachycardia or pre-excitation, not typical nodal re-entry.

options.text: Absent entirely — the atria are not depolarising
options.feedback: The atria are depolarising, retrogradely, on every beat of the circuit. The deflection is simply hidden.

options.text: Occurring at 300 per minute as flutter waves
options.feedback: There is no sawtooth baseline, and the ventricular rate of 186 does not fit a simple division of 300.

questions.explanation: Comparing the tachycardia tracing with the patient's own tracing in sinus rhythm afterwards is the classic way to reveal a hidden retrograde P wave.

questions.prompt: There is 1 mm of ST depression inferolaterally. What is the most appropriate way to report this?

options.text: Rate-related ST depression, to be reassessed once the rhythm has converted
options.feedback: Correct. ST depression during a fast supraventricular tachycardia is common, is often not ischaemic, and usually resolves on conversion.

options.text: Definite acute coronary syndrome
options.feedback: In a 27-year-old with no chest pain and no risk factors, calling this ischaemia on the tachycardic tracing alone would be wrong.

options.text: Normal, and not worth mentioning
options.feedback: It should be described, and reassessed afterwards — but described accurately as rate-related.

options.text: A digoxin effect
options.feedback: She takes no digoxin, and the scooped 'reverse tick' morphology is not present.

questions.explanation: Always repeat the ECG in sinus rhythm after a tachyarrhythmia. Changes that persist matter; changes that vanish usually did not.

questions.prompt: Taking the recurrent, abruptly starting episodes together with this tracing, what is the most likely interpretation?

options.text: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia due to atrioventricular nodal re-entry
options.feedback: Correct. Recurrent, self-limiting, abruptly starting and stopping episodes in a young patient with a structurally normal heart is the classic history.

options.text: Inappropriate sinus tachycardia
options.feedback: That is a persistent tachycardia disproportionate to activity, not discrete episodes with instantaneous onset and offset.

options.text: Panic disorder
options.feedback: Anxiety commonly accompanies these episodes and is often blamed for them — but the ECG shows a genuine re-entrant arrhythmia at 186 bpm.

options.text: Thyrotoxicosis
options.feedback: Thyrotoxicosis produces sinus tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, not a regular re-entrant tachycardia with abrupt onset.

questions.explanation: The history of abrupt onset and offset is diagnostically powerful. Ask about it in every patient with palpitations.

questions.prompt: The patient is alert with a systolic pressure of 106 mmHg. What is the appropriate first step in this educational scenario?

options.text: A vagal manoeuvre, such as the modified Valsalva
options.feedback: Correct. In a haemodynamically stable patient, vagal manoeuvres are first line, and the modified Valsalva with leg elevation is more effective than the standard technique.

options.text: Immediate unsynchronised defibrillation
options.feedback: Unsynchronised shocks are for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. This patient has a pulse and is stable.

options.text: Intravenous amiodarone as the first agent
options.feedback: Amiodarone is not first line for a stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia; vagal manoeuvres and then adenosine come first.

options.text: Observe for six hours without intervention
options.feedback: The rhythm can be terminated safely and simply, and prolonged tachycardia at 186 bpm is not benign.

questions.explanation: Educational scenario only. Follow current resuscitation council and society guidance, and escalate immediately if the patient becomes unstable.

explanation: In atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia the atrioventricular node contains two functionally distinct pathways with different conduction speeds and refractory periods. A well-timed atrial ectopic finds one pathway refractory, travels down the other, and returns up the first, establishing a self-sustaining circuit. Because both atria and ventricles are activated almost simultaneously, the retrograde P wave is buried in the QRS or distorts its terminal portion — the pseudo-R′ in V1. The circuit involves the node, which is why blocking the node with a vagal manoeuvre or adenosine terminates it, unlike atrial flutter where the circuit sits above the node.
learningObjectives: Recognise a regular narrow-complex tachycardia and reason about where the P waves have gone
Explain why nodal blockade terminates nodal re-entry but only unmasks flutter
Interpret rate-related ST depression cautiously and repeat the ECG after conversion
State the stepwise approach for a stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia
clinicalContext: The surface ECG cannot definitively distinguish nodal re-entry from an accessory-pathway tachycardia or an atrial tachycardia. That distinction is made by the response to adenosine, by comparing with a sinus tracing, and definitively by electrophysiological study.
